title: The Arabian Leopard
summary: The Arabian leopard, a rare big cat of the Arabian mountains, is in danger of dying out, and people across the region are working to save it.
poll: Saving a rare animal like the Arabian leopard is worth a lot of time and money.

versions.title: The Arabian Leopard
versions.text:
Meet the Arabian leopard. It is a big cat. It is wild. It is rare. It lives in high, dry mountains. They are in Saudi Arabia, Oman, and Yemen.

The cat has a gold coat. Its dark spots look like rings. It is the smallest leopard. But it is strong. It can jump far. It can climb rocks. It has a long tail.

This cat lives on its own. It sleeps in the day. It hunts at night. It hunts wild goats. They are called ibex. It eats gazelles, hares, and birds, too.

Now the cat is endangered. It may die out. Not a lot are left. Why? Roads and towns were built in its home. So its habitat got small. People hunted its prey, too. So the cat had less food.

Now we work hard to protect it. Some groups help the cats have cubs. The cubs are kept safe. One day, they may go back to the wild.

versions.title: A Rare Mountain Cat
versions.text:
The Arabian leopard is one of the rarest big cats in the world. It lives in the high, rocky mountains of Arabia. These are in parts of Saudi Arabia, Oman, and Yemen. Few people have ever seen one in the wild.

This leopard has a pale golden coat covered with dark spots. The spots are shaped like open rings. They help the leopard blend in with the rocks. It is the smallest kind of leopard. A male weighs about 30 kilograms. That is about the same as a ten-year-old child. Even so, it is a powerful hunter. It can leap great distances and climb steep cliffs.

The Arabian leopard usually lives alone. During the hot day, it often rests in caves or shady spots. It hunts mostly at night. Its main prey is the Nubian ibex. This is a wild goat with long, curved horns. It also hunts gazelles, hares, rock hyraxes, and birds.

Sadly, the Arabian leopard is endangered. This means it is in danger of dying out. Experts think fewer than 200 are left in the wild. There are two main reasons. First, people built roads, farms, and towns in the mountains. So the leopard's habitat got smaller. Second, people hunted many ibex and gazelles. That left the leopard with less prey to eat.

Today, people across the region are working to protect the leopard. In Saudi Arabia, a center in Taif helps leopards have cubs. The cubs are raised in a safe place. The goal is to return some of them to the wild one day.

versions.title: The Arabian Leopard: A Rare Mountain Cat
versions.text:
The Arabian leopard is one of the rarest big cats on the planet. It lives in the rugged mountains of the Arabian Peninsula. It is found in parts of Saudi Arabia, Oman, and Yemen. It is so shy and rare that few people have ever seen one in the wild. Most of the wild ones that remain are thought to live in Oman and Yemen.

This leopard has a pale golden coat decorated with dark, ring-shaped spots called rosettes. The pattern helps the leopard blend in with the rocky ground. It is the smallest kind of leopard. A grown male weighs about 30 kilograms, about the same as a ten-year-old child. Even so, it is a skilled predator. It can leap great distances and climb steep cliffs with ease.

Arabian leopards usually live alone. During the hottest part of the day, they often rest in caves or in the shade of rocks. They do most of their hunting at night. Their main prey is the Nubian ibex, a wild goat with long, curved horns. They also hunt gazelles, hares, rock hyraxes, and birds.

Sadly, the Arabian leopard is endangered. This means the species is at risk of dying out forever. Experts believe fewer than 200 remain in the wild. One reason is the loss of habitat. As people built roads, farms, and towns, the mountain home of the leopard grew smaller. It was broken into pieces. Another reason is the loss of prey. When people hunted too many ibex and gazelles, the leopards had less food. Some leopards were also killed by herders who wanted to protect their goats.

Today, people across the region are working hard to save this species. In Saudi Arabia, a breeding center in Taif helps leopards have cubs in a safe place. Scientists hope to release some of these animals back into protected mountain areas in the future.

They do most of their hunting at night. Their main prey is the Nubian ibex, a wild goat with long, curved horns. They also hunt gazelles, hares, rock hyraxes, and birds.

Unfortunately, the Arabian leopard is endangered. This means the species is at serious risk of disappearing forever. Experts estimate that fewer than 200 remain in the wild. versions.text:

During the hottest hours of the day, they typically shelter in caves or beneath overhanging boulders, and they do most of their hunting under the cover of night. versions.title: The Arabian Leopard: A Cat on the Edge
versions.text:
The Arabian leopard is among the rarest large cats on Earth. It inhabits the rugged mountain ranges of the Arabian Peninsula. It survives in scattered pockets of Saudi Arabia, Oman, and Yemen. Because it is secretive, exceedingly scarce, and primarily nocturnal, very few people have ever glimpsed one in its natural surroundings. Most of the surviving wild population is believed to live in Oman and Yemen.

The leopard's pale golden coat is decorated with dark, ring-shaped markings called rosettes. This pattern provides effective camouflage against the sun-bleached rocks. Scientists classify the Arabian leopard as a distinct subspecies, and it is the smallest variety of leopard in the world. An adult male weighs approximately 30 kilograms, roughly equivalent to a ten-year-old child, while females are considerably lighter. Despite its modest size, it is a formidable predator. It is capable of leaping impressive distances and scaling nearly vertical cliffs.

Arabian leopards are generally solitary, and each individual patrols an extensive territory. During the scorching daytime hours, they typically shelter in caves or beneath overhanging boulders, emerging after dark to hunt. Their primary prey is the Nubian ibex, a wild goat with long, curved horns, although they also pursue gazelles, hares, rock hyraxes, and birds.

Tragically, the Arabian leopard is classified as critically endangered. This means it faces an extremely high risk of extinction in the wild. Experts estimate that fewer than 200 individuals remain. The first major cause is habitat loss. As people constructed roads, farms, and settlements, the leopard's mountain home contracted and became divided into isolated fragments. The second cause is the decline of its prey. When ibex and gazelles were hunted excessively, the leopards were deprived of sufficient food. Some began attacking livestock instead. This created conflict with herders, some of whom killed leopards to protect their goats and camels.

Today, governments and scientists throughout the region are cooperating on conservation efforts. In Saudi Arabia, a breeding center in Taif helps leopards raise cubs in a secure environment, gradually increasing the population. Researchers also install hidden cameras along mountain trails to monitor wild leopards and identify where they still survive. Ultimately, they hope to reintroduce animals into protected mountain reserves, giving the species a genuine opportunity to recover. Each year, February 10 is observed as the International Day of the Arabian Leopard to raise public awareness.

versions.text:

It persists only in scattered, remote pockets of Saudi Arabia, Oman, and Yemen. Because it is secretive, exceedingly scarce, and predominantly nocturnal, remarkably few people have ever glimpsed one in its natural surroundings, and much of what scientists know comes from footprints, droppings, and photographs captured by concealed cameras. Most of the surviving wild population is believed to live in Oman and Yemen.

The leopard's pale golden coat is decorated with dark, ring-shaped markings called rosettes, a pattern that provides exceptionally effective camouflage against the sun-bleached limestone and granite of its habitat. Scientists classify the Arabian leopard as a distinct subspecies, and it is the smallest variety of leopard in the world. An adult male weighs approximately 30 kilograms, roughly equivalent to a ten-year-old child, while females are considerably lighter. Despite these modest dimensions, it is a formidable predator. It is capable of leaping impressive distances and scaling nearly vertical cliffs with extraordinary agility.

Arabian leopards are generally solitary, and each individual patrols an extensive territory that may stretch across numerous valleys and ridges. During the scorching daytime hours, they typically shelter in caves or beneath overhanging boulders, emerging after darkness falls to hunt. Their principal prey is the Nubian ibex, a wild goat with long, sweeping horns, although they also pursue gazelles, hares, rock hyraxes, and various birds.

Tragically, the Arabian leopard is classified as critically endangered. This signifies that it confronts an extremely high probability of extinction in the wild. Experts estimate that fewer than 200 individuals remain. The first major cause is habitat destruction: as people constructed highways, agricultural land, and expanding settlements, the leopard's mountain home contracted and fragmented into isolated patches, making it increasingly difficult for individuals to locate mates. The second cause is the dramatic decline of its prey. When ibex and gazelles were hunted excessively, the leopards were deprived of sufficient nourishment, and some resorted to attacking livestock instead. This generated bitter conflict with herders, some of whom retaliated by killing or poisoning leopards to defend their goats and camels.

Today, governments and scientists throughout the region are collaborating on ambitious conservation programs. In Saudi Arabia, a specialized breeding center in Taif helps leopards produce cubs in a secure environment, steadily enlarging the captive population. Researchers also conceal motion-activated cameras along mountain trails to monitor wild leopards and determine precisely which territories they still occupy. Ultimately, conservationists intend to reintroduce animals into protected mountain reserves where prey is plentiful, providing the species with a genuine opportunity to recover. Each year, February 10 is observed as the International Day of the Arabian Leopard to heighten public awareness of its plight.

versions.title: Protecting the Arabian Leopard
versions.text:
The Arabian leopard is among the rarest large cats remaining anywhere on Earth. It inhabits the rugged mountain ranges of the Arabian Peninsula, persisting only in scattered, remote pockets of Saudi Arabia, Oman, and Yemen. Because it is secretive, exceedingly scarce, and predominantly nocturnal in its habits, remarkably few people have ever glimpsed one in its natural surroundings, and much of what scientists currently understand about its behavior derives indirectly from footprints, droppings, and photographs captured by concealed cameras placed along mountain trails. Most of the surviving wild population is believed to persist today in the mountains of Oman and Yemen.

The leopard's pale golden coat is decorated with dark, ring-shaped markings called rosettes, a distinctive pattern that provides exceptionally effective camouflage against the sun-bleached limestone and granite that characterize its mountainous habitat. Scientists classify the Arabian leopard as a genetically distinct subspecies, and it is, by a considerable margin, the smallest variety of leopard found anywhere in the world. An adult male weighs approximately 30 kilograms, roughly equivalent to a ten-year-old human child, while adult females are considerably lighter still. Despite these comparatively modest physical dimensions, it remains a formidable and capable predator, fully able to leap impressive distances and ascend nearly vertical rock faces with extraordinary agility.

Arabian leopards are generally solitary animals, and each individual patrols an extensive territory that may encompass numerous separate valleys and ridgelines across the mountains. Throughout the scorching daytime hours, they typically shelter in caves or beneath overhanging boulders, emerging only after darkness descends in order to hunt. Their principal prey remains the Nubian ibex, an agile wild goat distinguished by long, sweeping horns, although they also pursue gazelles, hares, rock hyraxes, and various species of bird when the opportunity arises.

Tragically, the Arabian leopard is formally classified as critically endangered, signifying that it confronts an extremely high probability of complete extinction in the wild within a relatively short timeframe. Experts estimate that considerably fewer than 200 individuals remain alive today. The first fundamental cause of this decline is habitat destruction: as communities throughout the region constructed highways, agricultural developments, and expanding settlements, the leopard's mountain home contracted steadily and fragmented into isolated patches, making it increasingly difficult for individual leopards to encounter potential mates across these separated territories. The second principal cause is the dramatic decline of its natural prey base. When ibex and gazelles were hunted excessively by people over many decades, the leopards were deprived of sufficient nourishment, and some individuals resorted instead to attacking domestic livestock. This generated bitter and sometimes violent conflict with local herders, some of whom retaliated by killing or poisoning leopards in order to defend their goats and camels.

Today, governments and scientists throughout the region are collaborating closely on ambitious, long-term conservation programs. In Saudi Arabia, a specialized breeding center located in Taif enables leopards to produce cubs within a secure, carefully managed environment, steadily enlarging the overall captive population generation by generation. Researchers simultaneously conceal motion-activated cameras along remote mountain trails to monitor wild leopards and determine precisely which territories they continue to occupy. Ultimately, conservationists intend to reintroduce captive-bred animals into protected mountain reserves where prey populations have been deliberately restored beforehand, providing the species with a genuine opportunity for meaningful recovery. Each year, February 10 is observed internationally as the Day of the Arabian Leopard, an occasion specifically designed to heighten public awareness of its continuing precarious situation.

versions.title: Protecting the Arabian Leopard
versions.text:
The Arabian leopard is among the rarest large cats remaining anywhere on Earth today. It inhabits the rugged mountain ranges of the Arabian Peninsula, persisting only in scattered, remote pockets of Saudi Arabia, Oman, and Yemen that have thus far escaped significant human encroachment. Because it is secretive, exceedingly scarce, and predominantly nocturnal in virtually all of its habits, remarkably few people have ever glimpsed one in its natural surroundings, and much of what scientists currently understand about its behavior derives indirectly from footprints, droppings, and photographs captured by concealed cameras positioned along remote mountain trails. Most of the surviving wild population is believed to persist today specifically in the mountains of Oman and Yemen.

The leopard's pale golden coat is decorated with dark, ring-shaped markings called rosettes, a distinctive pattern that provides exceptionally effective camouflage against the sun-bleached limestone and granite that characterize its mountainous habitat throughout the year. Scientists classify the Arabian leopard as a genetically distinct subspecies within the broader leopard family, and it is, by a considerable margin, the smallest variety of leopard found anywhere in the world. An adult male weighs approximately 30 kilograms, roughly equivalent to the weight of a ten-year-old human child, while adult females are considerably lighter still, often by a substantial margin. Despite these comparatively modest physical dimensions relative to other big cats, it remains a formidable and highly capable predator, fully able to leap impressive distances across rocky terrain and ascend nearly vertical rock faces with truly extraordinary agility.

Arabian leopards are generally solitary animals by nature, and each individual patrols an extensive territory that may encompass numerous separate valleys and ridgelines scattered across the mountains. Throughout the scorching daytime hours, when temperatures can become dangerously high, they typically shelter in caves or beneath overhanging boulders, emerging only after darkness descends fully in order to hunt under cover. Their principal prey remains the Nubian ibex, an agile wild goat distinguished by long, sweeping horns adapted to similarly rugged terrain, although Arabian leopards also pursue gazelles, hares, rock hyraxes, and various species of bird whenever the opportunity presents itself.

Tragically, the Arabian leopard is formally classified as critically endangered, a designation signifying that it confronts an extremely high probability of complete extinction in the wild within a relatively short timeframe unless current trends are reversed. Experts estimate that considerably fewer than 200 individuals remain alive in the wild today, a staggeringly small number for an entire subspecies. The first fundamental cause of this precipitous decline is habitat destruction: as communities throughout the region constructed highways, agricultural developments, and steadily expanding settlements, the leopard's mountain home contracted considerably and fragmented into increasingly isolated patches, making it progressively more difficult for individual leopards to encounter potential mates across these now-separated territories. The second principal cause is the dramatic decline of its natural prey base across the same period. When ibex and gazelles were hunted excessively by people over many preceding decades, the leopards were deprived of sufficient nourishment to sustain themselves, and some individuals consequently resorted to attacking domestic livestock instead. This shift generated bitter, and at times genuinely violent, conflict with local herders, some of whom retaliated by killing or poisoning leopards in order to defend their goats and camels from perceived threats.

Today, governments and scientists throughout the region are collaborating closely on increasingly ambitious, long-term conservation programs designed to reverse this decline. In Saudi Arabia, a specialized breeding center located in Taif enables leopards to produce cubs within a secure, carefully managed environment, steadily enlarging the overall captive population generation after generation. Researchers simultaneously conceal motion-activated cameras along remote mountain trails across the region to monitor wild leopards and determine precisely which territories they continue to occupy under current conditions. Ultimately, conservationists intend to reintroduce captive-bred animals into protected mountain reserves where prey populations have first been deliberately restored, providing the species with a genuine, realistic opportunity for meaningful long-term recovery. Each year, February 10 is observed internationally as the Day of the Arabian Leopard, an occasion specifically designed to heighten sustained public awareness of its continuing and genuinely precarious situation.

LOW.modelAnswer: The Arabian leopard is endangered for a few reasons. As people built roads, farms, and towns, the leopard's mountain habitat got smaller and was cut into pieces. The leopards also lost prey, like the ibex and gazelles that people hunted too much. Now people are trying to protect the leopard so it does not disappear forever.

MID.prompt: The article names more than one cause for the leopard's decline. Which cause do you think is the most serious? Explain using details from the article.
checklist: I chose one cause and stated it clearly.
I used at least two details from the article to support my choice.
I explained how this cause affects the leopard.
MID.modelAnswer: I think the loss of prey is the most serious cause of the Arabian leopard's decline. This predator species depends on animals like the Nubian ibex and gazelles to survive, but the article explains that people hunted too many of these animals, leaving leopards without enough food to eat. Without enough prey, leopards with their beautiful rosette patterns may also wander closer to farms looking for food, which can lead herders to kill them while protecting their goats and camels. Because of this cause, a breeding center in Taif is now working to help the species recover.

HIGH.prompt: Conservationists hope to reintroduce Arabian leopards into the wild. What problems must they solve first for this plan to succeed? Use evidence from the article.
checklist: I named at least two problems that threaten leopards in the wild.
I explained how each problem could be solved, using evidence from the article.
I organized my answer clearly, with a beginning, middle, and end.
HIGH.modelAnswer: Before conservationists can successfully reintroduce Arabian leopards into the wild, they must solve at least two serious problems described in the article. First, this nocturnal subspecies has lost much of its mountain habitat to roads, farms, and towns, so any released leopards would need enough connected, undisturbed territory to hunt safely at night. Second, the leopards' main prey, like ibex and gazelles, has been overhunted, and without solving this food shortage, reintroduced leopards might wander toward livestock and be killed by herders protecting their animals, just as has happened before. Conservation programs like the breeding center in Taif are a hopeful beginning, but only once habitat is protected and prey populations recover will reintroduction truly give the species a chance to survive in the wild.
